28.0.0.en: 1 Whoever takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord, and the Lord will keep a close watch on his sins.

28.0.1.en: Vengeance is among the first sins that man practiced (Gen 4:14-15, 23-24). Sirach begins by observing that those who seek vengeance on their brethren are themselves called to account for the errors and sins they have committed. It was said of Cain: "Whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold" (Gen 4:15).

28.0.2.en: Whoever seeks vengeance will be overtaken by the vengeance of the Lord, who will surely punish him for his sins [1].

28.0.3.en: The Book of Deuteronomy recorded the same concept: "To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste" (Deut 32:35), and the Apostle Paul confirmed it: "Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19).

28.0.4.en: St. Basil the Great stands amazed as he looks at man in his state of agitation. He loses his natural characteristics as a human being, even his features change, and he becomes like another person.

28.0.5.en: One wonders: has the man been transformed into a beast, or has a demon entered him and changed his whole being?!

28.0.6.en: v Who can describe such an evil accurately?! How the quick-tempered, as soon as some pretext chances to seize them, cry out and shout and attack with a shame no less than the shame of the brute or of the beast that breathes out venom! Nothing stops such a person until immense harm that cannot be remedied has occurred, as if a bubble of wrath were bursting and boiling, pouring out scorching waves without restraint. Neither the edge of a sword, nor fire, nor anything else terrifying can stop and restrain a soul driven headlong by the madness of anger.

28.0.7.en: No one is able to restrain those possessed by demons; so the wrathful are no different from them, either in appearance or in the inclinations of their souls.

28.0.8.en: For those who long for vengeance, the blood boils in their hearts, as if it were kindling and breathing out as from a raging, blazing fire. They burst out and their anger appears for all to see, so that the angry man looks different from the man everyone knows and is accustomed to, as if he had put on his face a mask like that worn by one who stands on a stage. Those near him do not see in his eyes those usual expressions, but the marks of madness appear in his gaze, and fires blaze in his eyes. He grinds his teeth like a wild boar going out to battle. His face becomes flushed and full of blood, his body swells and grows heavy, and his blood vessels burst. His breathing quickens savagely, as though a storm were raging within him. His voice rises and trembles and reaches the utmost pitch, and no one understands what he says; it pours out without restraint, rushing along without order or logic and without clarity [1].

28.1.0.en: 2 Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done you; then when you pray, your sins will be forgiven. 3 Does a man harbor anger against another man, and then seek healing from the Lord? 4 Or does he not show mercy to a man like himself, and then ask forgiveness for his own sins? 5 If he, being flesh, holds on to resentment, who will atone for his sins? 6 Remember your last end, and cease from enmity. 7 Remember corruption and death, and abide in the commandments. 8 Remember the commandments, and do not bear malice toward your neighbor. 9 Remember the covenant of the Most High, and overlook ignorance.

28.1.1.en: Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has committed, and your sins will be forgiven when you pray [2].

28.1.2.en: Ben Sira does not ask the wise man merely to refrain from vengeance; he requires him to forgive the one who worked to harm him, so that God may hear him and forgive his sins [2]. As the Lord Christ teaches us to pray: "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" (Mt 6:12). The Lord Christ comments on this prayer: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: but if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses" (Mt 6:15). The Lord Christ made this principle clear by the parable of the servant who would not forgive his fellowservant (Mt 18:23-25).

28.1.3.en: Truly God, who is all love and mercy, longs to forgive us our sins, but if we do not forgive our brethren we shall not enjoy the divine love. Our insistence on taking vengeance on those who oppose us hides from us the enjoyment of the spirit of love and humility, and so we are deprived of receiving God's mercies toward us.

28.1.4.en: v The believer must not be angry with his neighbor without cause, nor harbor wrath against anyone, nor return evil for evil. It befits him to be reviled rather than to revile, to be struck rather than to strike, to be wronged rather than to do wrong, and to be robbed rather than to rob [2].

28.2.0.en: St. Basil the Great Does a man keep hatred against his neighbor, and then seek healing from the Lord? [3]

28.2.1.en: Whoever keeps hatred is struck with a grave sickness that deprives him of healing from his sins.

28.2.2.en: v God prefers love above everything. As in the making of the royal purple robe the flowers and the dye from which the color of the robe is made are counted the most precious thing, so nothing supports love like our not remembering the faults of those who oppose us... It is sweeter to love a person who has wronged us than to hate him [3].

28.3.0.en: v Why do we imitate madmen, each devouring the other, and wage war against our own bodies? Hear what the Old Testament says, how greatly it concerns itself with this matter: "The ways of the avengers lead to death" (see Prov 12:28) LXX. "Does a man harbor anger against another man, and then seek healing from the Lord?" (see Sir 28:3) [4]

28.4.0.en: v Do not be wrathful with anyone, and do not bear a grudge, forgiving all their transgressions. For it is said: "Does a man harbor anger against another man, and then seek healing from the Lord?" (see Sir 28:3). "Forgive, and ye shall be forgiven" (Mk 11:25) [5].

28.4.1.en: St. John Chrysostom Can he refrain from showing mercy to a man like himself, and then ask mercy for himself from God? [4]

28.4.2.en: In the parable of the Lord Christ in which He declares the universal fall of human nature (Mt 18:23-35), He calls us to show gentleness to the fallen, so that God may show gentleness to us.

28.4.3.en: If he continually holds on to wrath, being flesh, who will atone for his sins? [5]

28.5.0.en: v It is fitting and very honorable for a man to practice Christianity and not to demand the blood of his adulterous (wife); we cite to him what is written: "Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done you, and when you pray your sins will be forgiven. Does a man harbor anger against another, and then seek healing from the Lord? Or does he not show mercy to a man like himself, and then pray for the forgiveness of his sins? If he, being flesh, holds on to resentment, who will atone for his sins?" (see Sir 28:2-5). By this we can say: "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" (Mt 6:12). And it is said in the Apostle: "Recompense to no man evil for evil" (Rom 12:17) [6].

28.5.1.en: St. Augustine Remember the end of your life, and cease from enmity; remember destruction and death, and abide in the commandments [6].

28.5.2.en: The practical way to calm the soul from the desire for vengeance is to remember death and the day of judgment. The Holy Bible and the Fathers of the Church urge us to meditate on the day of our departure and our meeting with Christ on the great day of judgment.

28.5.3.en: v The remembrance of death is good (Sir 28:6; 41:1), so that man may know that he is mortal and realize that the mortal is not eternal. For he who is not eternal will surely leave this age, even against his will. Therefore, by the constant remembrance of death, man learns to do good by his own free will [6].

28.6.0.en: St. Barsanuphius and St. John Remember the commandments, and do not vent your wrath on your neighbor; remember the covenant of the Most High, and overlook faults [7].

28.6.1.en: It befits the believer, through his love for the salvation of all humanity as his brethren, to look at the one who wrongs him as a sick man who needs love, tenderness, kindness and calm as medicines to help him toward the salvation of his soul. In the same spirit St. Augustine invites us to look at the one who wrongs us as a little child stricken with fever, whom we treat gently and are not vexed with, but embrace until he is healed of it.

28.6.2.en: v The doer of evil must be treated as by a physician, who is not angry with the sick man but fights the sickness. So vice is attacked and the weakness of the soul is corrected... For example, pride is corrected by being required to practice humility, idle talk by silence, laziness by work, gluttony by abstinence from food, and murmuring by withdrawal from the company of the brethren [7].

28.7.s.en: 3. Ceasing from strife and evil speech

28.7.0.en: 10 Refrain from strife, and you will lessen sins. 11 For a hot-tempered man kindles strife, and a sinful man disturbs friends, and casts discord among those who are at peace. 12 As the wood of the fire, so it burns; and according to a man's strength is his wrath; and according to his wealth he increases his anger; and according to the vehemence of the strife it blazes. 13 A hasty quarrel kindles a fire, and a hasty dispute sheds blood. 14 If you blow on a spark, it will glow; and if you spit on it, it will be put out; and both come out of your mouth.

28.7.1.en: Avoid quarreling, and you will lessen your sins, for the violent-tempered man kindles quarreling [8].

28.7.2.en: v Drive away by your silence the darkness of the wrathful man whom you see, and you will again acquire joy in your heart, and peace among the brethren, men and women, who are like you in mind, and zeal and care for keeping the churches of the Lord [8].

28.7.3.en: v Do not treat evil with evil, and do not try to overcome one another in such matters. For in the strife to gain the victory by evil, the victor is always wretched and miserable, for he departs bearing with him his greater sin. For this reason he who repays evil with evil does not become perfect... Stop evil by silence! But when you receive into your heart the storm of that person's anger, you imitate the wind, and strike back at what has blown upon you with a counterblow. Do not use your enemy as a teacher, while you hate him! Do not imitate him in this. Do not be, so to speak, a mirror of the one rushing in anger, showing within yourself the same appearance as his.

28.7.4.en: His color has turned red; do you want your color to be like the color of wine? His eyes are red as burning coals [9].

28.7.5.en: v He who is chaste in the desire for honor is also humble. He who is chaste in wealth is content, and attains the measure of the Gospel in poverty. He who controls indignation and anger is gentle. Truly the observance of true chastity governs the tongue, sets a limit for the eyes, and cleanses the ears from listening to gossip out of curiosity. But he who does not keep all this is not chaste but unrestrained [10].

28.7.6.en: v He who uses his intelligence and skill to destroy others is wicked; but he who works with intelligence and firmness to avoid the harms that others store up for him recognizes wisely what is for his good, acquiring praiseworthy prudence.

28.8.0.en: Listen diligently to the voice of the prudent soul, and you will know that it has a center that uses prudence to give sound counsel to itself as well as to its neighbor, and this is praiseworthy [11].

28.8.1.en: St. Basil the Great The sinful man troubles his friends and sows discord among those who are at peace [9].

28.9.0.en: The fire burns according to the amount of wood; so also the fire burns according to the stubbornness of the quarrel [12].

28.9.1.en: And according to a man's strength is his anger, and according to his wealth his indignation increases [10].

28.9.2.en: v The man who makes peace with another immediately after rising up against him heals his anger but does not heal his grudge; therefore he remains resentful toward his brother. For anger is one thing, grudge is another, agitation (upheaval) a third, and disturbance yet another.

28.9.3.en: And so that you may understand the matter more clearly, I give you an example: in order to kindle a fire a man takes a piece of coal, and this is the word with which your brother wronged you; if you bear it, you will have put out the coal. But if you think: "Why does he say this to me? I too will answer him by saying such and such. If he had not intended to wrong me he would not have said this to me. Therefore I must repay the wrong in kind." By this thinking you put some fuel or the like to start the fire. And thereby it produces smoke, which is disturbance. And disturbance is a movement in the thoughts and a turning of them over, which stirs up the heart and agitates it.

28.9.4.en: Agitation, however, is a vengeful act against the one who wronged you. And this leads to boldness. St. Mark said: "Ill will, when fed by thoughts, agitates the heart, but prayer kills it."

28.9.5.en: Yet if you had borne those little words that your brother uttered, you would have put out the little piece of coal before it produced disturbance. And even so, if you wish, you can put out even the disturbance at its beginning by silence and prayer, and even by merely bowing from the heart. But if you persist in fanning the smoke, that is, in agitating the heart and stirring it up with thoughts that say: "Why did he do this to me?.. and I will repay him in kind," then by this the heart is kindled and the flame of agitation is generated. And if you wish, you can also put out the agitation before it reaches anger.

28.10.0.en: But if you persist in stirring yourself up and agitating yourself, you are like one who adds fuel to the fire. And so you produce a blaze, which is anger. And anger, if it continues, turns into a grudge, from which man cannot be freed except by shedding his blood (that is, his sweat and effort and the toil of his soul) [13].

28.10.1.en: Abba Dorotheus v Question: What is the difference between bitterness, wrath, anger and clamor (Eph 4:31; Ps 58:5)?

28.11.0.en: Answer: The difference between wrath and anger, I think, lies in the inclination and the impulse, since the pain of the one who is moved to anger extends only to the inclination (or disposition), as the one who says: "Be ye angry, and sin not" (Ps 4:5; Eph 4:26) clearly shows. But the wrathful man, his impulse extends, since it is said of the wrathful that he is like the serpent (Ps 58:5). Herod was wrathful toward Tyre and Sidon (Acts 12:20). The extension of wrath reaches to clamor, and bitterness is declared with exceedingly terrible determination, with deliberate malice in the heart (Eph 4:31) [14].

28.11.1.en: v Anger makes brothers ignore one another, and fathers and sons forget the natural bond between them. For wrathful persons begin by ignoring themselves first, and then in truth ignore all their friends. Just as torrents rush down from the top of a mountain and sweep away before them everything in the valleys that stands in their way, so fits of anger that are hard to control sweep away before them everyone who stands in their way. Those possessed by wrath do not respect the aged, nor care for the life of goodness, nor are they concerned with the strong tie of kinship, nor with the kindnesses that people had done them before, nor with anything else honorable.

28.12.0.en: Wrath is a kind of short-lived madness. The angry often harm themselves in their rush toward vengeance, heedless of their own interests. For as soon as they remember those who grieved them, they appear like men stung by horseflies all over their bodies, so that their wrath is stirred up and leaps within them, and they do not rest until they do something that harms the one who provoked them, and perhaps they themselves receive the harm, just as things violently shattered suffer more severe damage than they would cause when they strike against hard objects [15].

28.12.1.en: St. Basil the Great A hasty dispute kindles a fire, and a quarrel in zeal sheds blood [11].

28.12.2.en: If you blow on a spark it will glow, but if you spit on it it will be put out, and both come out of your mouth [12].

28.12.3.en: Whoever does not flee from the atmosphere of quarreling finds his heart growing more inflamed toward vengeance. And the fires of anger blaze upon his tongue, so that he begins with violent speech, like a spark of which we do not know how far it will inflame the fires of vengeance (Jas 3:5-6).

28.12.4.en: St. Basil presents to us the cycle of anger; for often the inner feelings of anger turn into conflict and quarreling, and quarreling begets faults, and faults drive to blows, and blows cause wounds, and wounds may drive to death. Stopping anger in its first early stages is far easier than stopping it in its later stages.

28.12.5.en: How do you stop anger at the start of its stages? Remember that what someone insults you with is in reality not an insult, for Abraham, the father of fathers, said of himself that he was dust and ashes, and David reckoned himself a worm and no man. Let us imitate Moses, whom Aaron and Miriam wronged: instead of thinking of the insult that had come upon him, he prayed for them.

28.12.6.en: v Tell me, does calm show on your countenance? His voice trembles; is your own voice gentle?

28.12.7.en: For the echo of a voice in the wilderness is not like what he does who answers the one who wrongs him. On the contrary, the echo answers only a word with a word like it, whereas he who wrestles with another answers him with further words in addition. For what is the nature of the words that quarrelers say together? One says to the other that he is a worthless person, the son of a worthless man, and the other answers that he is a slave, the son of a slave.

28.12.8.en: One says: He is a poor laborer, and the other says: You vagabond!

28.12.9.en: One says: You fool, and the other answers: You madman.

28.12.10.en: And so they exchange insults between them like rebounding arrows. These are the abuses of the tongue that hasten on, and soon vengeance comes upon them through deeds. For wrath begets conflict and quarreling, and quarreling begets fault, and fault begets blows, and blows beget wounds, and wounds often lead to death.

28.13.0.en: So let us stop evil from the very beginning, very early! Let us remove anger from our souls with every possible effort. By this we can uproot many evils together with the passions, for evil is a kind of root, a kind of source [16].

28.13.1.en: v Has he spat upon you and counted you as nothing? Receive this thought concerning him, that you are taken from the dust of the earth, and that you will return to the earth and the dust (Gen 3:19). He who applies this thought to himself, truly and from his heart, finds that every contempt toward him is less than the truth. By this you give your enemy no opportunity for vengeance, and you show him that the insult does not shake you. So you gain for yourself a great crown of perseverance, making another's madness the starting point of your wisdom. For this reason, if you listen to his anger, you will of your own will add further insults to yourself...

28.14.0.en: Does someone call you a fool and a beggar who deserves nothing? Say that you yourself are a "worm" (Ps 23:6), and born of the mire of a "dunghill," as David said [17].

28.15.0.en: 15 The whisperer and the double-tongued are deserving of a curse, for they have destroyed many who were at peace. 16 The third tongue has disquieted many, and scattered them from nation to nation, 17 and has pulled down strong cities, and overthrown the houses of the great, 18 and has broken the armies of peoples, and destroyed mighty nations. 19 The third tongue has driven out virtuous women, and deprived them of their labors. 20 Whoever listens to it will find no rest, and will not dwell in security. 21 The stroke of a whip leaves a welt, but the stroke of the tongue breaks bones. 22 Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not so many as have fallen by the tongue. 23 Blessed is he who is sheltered from its evil, who has not been exposed to its wrath, who has not borne its yoke and has not been bound with its bonds, 24 for its yoke is a yoke of iron, and its bonds are bonds of bronze. 25 Death by it is a cruel death, and Hades is better than it. 26 But it has no power over the godly, and they will not be burned by its flame, 27 but those who forsake the Lord fall under its power, and it will burn among them and not be quenched. It will be sent against them like a lion, and it will devour them like a leopard. 28 Fence in your property with thorns. 29 Lock up your silver and gold, and make a balance and a weight for your words, and a door and a bolt for your mouth, 30 and take heed lest you slip by it, and fall before one who lies in wait for you.

28.15.1.en: Anger causes loss of control over the will and over the senses and the body, especially the tongue. When it rises in the mind or the heart it makes a man lose control over his tongue, so that he utters speech without restraint, and the members of his body rise up in a spirit of violence, and he carries within him the stirrings of mockery and bodily violence, and thus countless evil deeds are begotten from anger and wrath! In short, anger deprives of freedom and makes of itself a maidservant (a slave) without authority!

28.16.0.en: v Anger makes tongues unbridled and speech without restraint. Likewise bodily violence, acts of mockery, abuse, accusations, blows and other countless evil deeds are born of anger and wrath [18].

28.17.0.en: v Because of anger tongues are not bridled, lips are not silenced, hands are not bound, but from anger and its passions, and from wrath and its feelings, there are begotten countless agitations, uproars, rebukes, slanders, blows and other things without number. By wrath also the edge of the sword is sharpened, and the hand of man dares to kill a man [19].

28.17.1.en: St. Basil the Great Curse the slanderer and the deceiver, for he destroys many of those who are at peace [13].

28.17.2.en: The lack of control over the tongue kindles the spark all the more. Many nations have been completely shattered because of a small spark that came from an uncontrolled tongue.

28.17.3.en: Gossip unsettles many and scatters them from nation to nation, and pulls down strong cities and overturns the houses of the great [14].

28.17.4.en: v Envy is the germ and root of evils; from it spring murder, hatred, slander, plunder, desiring harm for others, and the like. Which of you does not know that by envy one imitates the devil, through whose envy death entered into the world?

28.17.5.en: St. John Chrysostom Gossip drives out virtuous women and deprives them of the fruits of their labors [15].

28.17.6.en: King Ahasuerus listened to the gossip of the drunken and drove out Queen Vashti, the virtuous (Esth 1:17).

28.17.7.en: Whoever devotes himself to gossip finds no rest and will not dwell in security [16].

28.17.8.en: v What does it mean to abstain from eating meat while we do not abstain from eating the flesh of our neighbor by gossip and backbiting? And what does it mean to fast from food while we do not cease from evil thoughts, fornication, grudges and hatred?

28.18.0.en: Beware of fasting only from meat and thinking that this is what is required of you. True fasting is abstaining from every vice: "Put away all iniquity" (Isa 8:5), and it is the forgiveness of every offense against the neighbor; it is the remission of debts owed by the needy: do not fast in order to quarrel and to go to law before the courts [20].

28.18.1.en: St. Basil the Great v Could we perhaps find another man like the Apostle Paul, who could say: "I have a desire to depart, and to be with Christ" (Phil 1:23)?

28.19.0.en: For my part I cannot speak as Paul did, for I know that if I depart, all that is wood, hay and stubble (1 Cor 3:12) in me must be burned. This wood that is in me is gossip, excess in drinking, thefts and other kinds of wood that have piled up upon the foundation that is in my house. All this is hidden from many believers; each one of us thinks that so long as he has not committed adultery or fornication he will be saved; and we do not realize that "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad" (2 Cor 5:10). And we do not set before us Him who said: "You only have I known of all the tribes of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities" (Amos 3:2), not for some of your iniquities while for the others I will not punish you [21].

28.19.1.en: Origen The stroke of a whip causes a wound, and the stroke of the tongue breaks bones [17].

28.19.2.en: Some think that words cause them no harm, but practical experience reveals how dangerous the lack of control over the tongue is, for it has shattered people, families and nations.

28.19.3.en: Many fall by the edge of the sword, but they are not as many as those who fall because of the tongue [18].

28.19.4.en: v If only we could see how our inner man has been wounded by every sin!... Have you not read: Swords wound, but not as the tongue wounds [18]. Therefore the soul is wounded by the tongue, as also by evil thoughts and wicked lusts, for it is broken and shattered by the works of sin. If we were able to see all these things and perceive the scars of the wounded soul, we would surely resist sin unto death.

28.20.0.en: In any case, just as those who suffer delirium and loss of their senses do not feel that they are wounded, because they have lost their natural sensations, so we cannot feel the gravity of our wounds and the extent of the soul's misery that sin causes, if we are struck with the madness of the love of worldly pleasures and the drunkenness of vice [22].

28.20.1.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles Blessed is the man who is sheltered from it, and is not exposed to the wrath of the tongue, and does not draw its yoke, and is not bound with its bonds [19].

28.20.2.en: For its yoke is a yoke of iron, and its bonds are bonds of bronze [20].

28.20.3.en: Death by it is an evil death, and Hades is better than it [21].

28.20.4.en: The evil tongue has no power over the godly, and they will not be burned by its flame [22].

28.20.5.en: Godliness, or the fear of the Lord, delivers a man from the yoke of the tongue and its bondage [22-26]. If a man does not master his tongue, the tongue masters him; or he who does not enslave his tongue, his tongue enslaves him.

28.20.6.en: Those who forsake the Lord fall under its power, and it will burn among them and not be quenched.

28.21.0.en: It will be sent against them like a lion, and will devour them like a leopard [23].

28.21.1.en: Just as the farmer protects his property with a fence, so it befits the wise man to guard his tongue from slander. Careless persons who slip by their tongues fall prey to onlookers (Prov 13:3; 21:23).

28.22.0.en: Behold, fence in your property with thorns, and lock up your silver and gold [24].

28.22.1.en: Every morning the believer asks: "Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth; keep my lips" (see Ps 141:3).

28.22.2.en: v Beloved brother Andrew, listen: those who receive pure, unalloyed coins from the king, if they keep them with zeal and care, find that they retain their luster and cleanness. But if they do not take care of them, they are not only soiled but perhaps even lost. For this reason one of the wise said: "Bind up your gold and silver" (see Sir 28:24).

28.22.3.en: I tell you not only to bind them with unwavering faith, but also to seal them with humility and longsuffering, with the patience by which he who endures is saved. I tell you a bold thing, by God who permits me to do so: the Lord Jesus, the great Mediator, the Son of the blessed Father, the Giver of the life-giving Holy Spirit, tells you through me, the last of all: "Your many sins are forgiven you" (Lk 5:20; 7:48), your sins from your birth until now! By receiving this great and unspeakable joy, you love Him with all your power, bringing forth fruits meet for repentance (Mt 3:8) [23].

28.22.4.en: St. Barsanuphius and St. John v Let everyone welcome fasting with zeal as the mother of all sanctification, mortification and subjection of the body (1 Cor 9:27), and choose to undertake this work: he fences his property with thorns [24], as one of our wise men says [24].

28.22.5.en: Pope St. Cyril the Great v Beloved brethren, let us courageously avoid and shun the words of those whose speech spreads as a gangrene (2 Tim 2:17), and as the Apostle says: "Evil communications corrupt good manners" (1 Cor 14:33). So the wise man warns us: Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to the evil tongue [24] [25].

28.22.6.en: St. Cyprian the Martyr v For whom was it written: "Fence in your property with thorns, and lock up your silver and gold. And make a balance and a weight for your words, and a door and a bolt for your mouth" [24-25]?

28.22.7.en: Your property is your mind, your gold is your heart, and your silver is your speech. "The words of the Lord are pure words, as silver refined in a furnace (by fire)" (Ps 12:6). A good mind is good property. Accordingly the pure inner life is valuable property. Fence this property, then, with thought; guard it with thorns, that is, with godly care, lest the ravening passions of the flesh rush upon it and take it captive, and violent emotions attack it, and transgress its boundaries and carry off its vines.

28.23.0.en: Guard your inner life. Do not neglect it, and do not hold it lightly as though it were trivial, for it is valuable property. Truly it is precious; its fruits do not perish after only a while, but remain to be used for eternal salvation [26].

28.24.0.en: v Bind your words lest they run in rashness and become loose, and sins return through much speaking. Let them be restricted and so return to their limits. For the river that overflows quickly gathers mud... The sobriety of the mind has a bridle that restrains it, leads it and directs it [27].

28.24.1.en: St. Ambrose Make a balance and a weight for your words, and a door and a bolt for your mouth [25].

28.24.2.en: St. Cyprian the Martyr sees that the believer fences his ears from the poisons of the heretics by withdrawing from those who fled from the Church. The Apostle commands us: "Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us" (2 Thess 3:6). For there can be no fellowship between the faith and the enemy.

28.25.0.en: He who is not with Christ is against Christ, and is an enemy of His unity and peace, and cannot be united with us. If they come with prayers and correction, let them be heard; but if they attack with curses and threats, let them be rejected [28].

28.25.1.en: v It is clear that we defile ourselves when we speak everything that passes through our mind and talk about matters that ought not to be discussed, so that they become a source of sins, although we know that it befits our lips to be closed with understanding (Prov 15:7), and it befits us to make a balance and a weight for our words [25] [29].

28.26.0.en: Origen v "Shut your door" (Isa 26:20) in the face of the enemy. "Weigh your words in a balance, and make a bolt for your door" (see Sir 28:25). You know how I speak to you, so understand the things I say. Labor to make them firm, and you will find the treasures hidden in them according to God, and give in them fruit worthy of God, and do not put my gray hairs to shame, as I pray for you day and night. May God grant you to understand and to act in His fear, Amen [30].

28.26.1.en: v Cross over from this world, go up now to the Cross; rise above the earth, shake off the dust from your feet (Mt 10:14), despise the shame (Heb 12:2). Do not join the Chaldeans in kindling the fires of the furnace, lest you be burned with them (Dan 3:23) by the wrath of God. Esteem every person better than yourself (Phil 2:3), weep for your dead (Sir 22:11).. bind your words firmly in the yoke, and make a bolt for your door (see Sir 28:25) [31].

28.26.2.en: St. Barsanuphius and St. John v Put a door and a bolt on the mouth (see Sir 28:25). For countless evils come from idle talk: families are destroyed, friendships are torn apart, and endless tragedies occur. O man, do not busy yourself with the affairs of your neighbor. But you talk much, and there is weakness in you. Speak of your faults before God. Thus weakness is turned into no weakness, and even into profit. Speak of your weaknesses to your friends who are truly friends and godly, and in whom you trust, that they may pray for your sins. If you speak of the faults of others you will gain nothing and acquire nothing, but you will destroy yourself [32].

28.26.3.en: v Let us ask His help that we may complete our diligence in action, and keep our mouth, making a bolt for our mind, not always closed, but to be opened at the proper time... Therefore the wise Solomon says: "A time to keep silence, and a time to speak" (Eccl 3:3). If it were necessary for the mouth to be always open, it would not need a door; and if it were necessary for it to be always closed, it would not need a guard. The door and the guard are so that everything may be done in its time. Another says: "Make a balance and a weight for your words" (see Sir 28:29), that is, that we utter our words with care, weighing them and reflecting upon them [33].

28.26.4.en: St. John Chrysostom v Let your mouth have a door that is closed, and at need is lifted. Let it be shut tightly, so that no one can provoke your voice to anger, so that you return insult for insult [34].

28.26.5.en: St. Ambrose And take heed lest you slip by your tongue, lest you fall prey before one who lies in wait for you [26].

28.26.6.en: One way to avoid sins is to flee from disputes, for the man who loves quarreling tears friendships apart (Prov 15:18; 16:28). Quarrelers put fuel on the fire (Prov 26:20-21; Jas 3:5-6), especially if they are rich and men of authority (8:1-3; 13:2), and quarrels may lead to bloodshed (22:24; 27:15).

28.27.0.en: v You gave the first man dominion over all the earthly creation, not that he might display his might, but that he might enjoy Your care for him.

28.27.1.en: In my stubbornness I lost love, tenderness and mercy, for Your holy image has vanished from my depths.

28.27.2.en: Instead of grieving over what I have corrupted, the love of vengeance and pride have mastered my feelings and my will.

28.27.3.en: Our love of vengeance makes us worthy that vengeance be taken on us!

28.27.4.en: By our love of vengeance we rob You of Your work, for You say: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19).

28.27.5.en: v Turn my eyes away from the doings of my brethren, that I may see my own sins, and seek mercy for them and for myself.

28.27.6.en: Open my heart to love, that I may find sweet the tenderness toward the fallen.

28.27.7.en: Let me be angry at my sins and the sins of my brethren and not be angry at them, for we all await Your mercy.

28.27.8.en: Let me hate the sickness, not the sick man, for there is no man who is not exposed to sickness.

28.27.9.en: v Train me to flee from quarreling by holy silence. Then my heart will rejoice in Your wondrous work in sinners!

28.27.10.en: Let my heart be released from the battles of the world, and let it join the choir of the heavenly ones.

28.27.11.en: Instead of entering into disputes and argument, let me seek through love peace, joy and grace for my brethren and for myself!

28.27.12.en: Cleanse me completely, so that I do not waste my time in quarrels, nor my ears in listening to anger.

28.27.13.en: v Instead of throwing fuel on the fires of anger, grant me to pour out the waters of love, kindness and tenderness.

28.27.14.en: Do not allow anger to turn into a grudge, nor the grudge into agitation, nor the agitation into vengeance, but by Your Holy Spirit extinguish in me every unseemly passion.

28.27.15.en: The sweetness of fellowship with You, O my God, removes the bitterness of my anger against my brother!

28.27.16.en: v Instead of blowing with my mouth on the spark of anger, grant me to spit with my mouth on the spark so that it is put out!

28.27.17.en: Grant me to imitate Moses the prophet, who prayed for Aaron and Miriam who had insulted him (Num 12:13).

28.27.18.en: v Grant that my tongue may not move in my anger, and set a guard from You over my inner tongue.

28.27.19.en: O Lord, extinguish the spark of my tongue at the beginning of its starting, lest it turn into a deadly furnace.

28.27.20.en: Remove from me the wood of gossip, lest I be burned by it.

28.27.21.en: v Keep me from my tongue, and protect me from its harsh yoke, and free me from its bitter bonds, and extinguish the fire of its wrath!

28.27.22.en: May You sanctify it, that it may be made worthy to praise with the heavenly ones.

28.27.23.en: If You tame it, it pours out sweetness, gentleness and kindness.

28.27.24.en: And if it is not tamed, it devours me like a lion or a leopard.

28.27.25.en: Fence my mouth with Your grace, that no wounding word may come out of it; v set, O Lord, a guard from You over my mouth.

28.27.26.en: That I may know when to speak and when to be silent.

28.27.27.en: If I speak, grant that You may speak through me; and if I am silent, may You be revealed within me.
